scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated on American plantations during the slavery era as a way for enslaved people to practice military drills.
An 18th-century watercolor, 'The Old Plantation,' provides the earliest visual record, showing the dance being performed in South Carolina between Columbia and Orangeburg.
It was a communal activity where slaves gathered around competitive fighters to provide rhythmic support.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally, the dance was a clandestine method for practicing combat and military drills.
It served as a form of resistance and physical preparation.
It also functioned as a competitive social event where fighters could demonstrate skill.
Today it is a historical tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers use a stick or cane as a central prop, which historically served as a disguised weapon.
The performance involves competitive fighting elements and acrobatic moves.
In later minstrel versions, the dancer would start with a slow shuffle as an elderly character before transitioning into high-energy, capoeira-like maneuvers.
Watch for The Cane Transformation.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Performed within a circle of people gathering around the fighters.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is traditionally provided by the banjo and drums.
The berimbau, based on African instruments, was also developed by African-American slaves for use in these contexts.
Listen for the Banjo, Drum, Berimbau, Sticks.

The sound is dominated by the percussive strike of sticks and rhythmic hand clapping. A lead caller provides a vocal melody that the crowd answers, backed by the sharp, twanging strings of a banjo and steady drumming.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Early depictions show the dance performed in front of slave cabins on plantations.
In the 19th-century minstrel tradition, the dancer often wore a costume depicting an elderly man, using a cane that would eventually be used for acrobatics.
Women in early depictions are shown dancing with scarves nearby.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The sources do not name specific individual dancers, but identify the anonymous subjects of 'The Old Plantation' watercolor as the earliest documented practitioners.
The dance is specifically associated with the South Carolina region, particularly between Columbia and Orangeburg.
The dance is a subclass of weapon dance.
